title: Midwinter Festivals
tagline: How the darkest days of the year have been marked from Rome to Japan.
intro: The winter solstice gives the Northern Hemisphere its shortest day and longest night on 21 or 22 December, and festivals have marked it since prehistory as the point when daylight begins to increase again. These stops follow that season across Eurasia: the Roman Saturnalia, the Yule of the heathen Germanic peoples, which later merged with Christmas, and the Slavic koliada, some of whose rituals date to pre-Christian times. They then turn to Yalda Night in Iran, the bonfires of Lohri in Punjab and Dongzhi in China, and end with Ōmisoka, the last day of the Japanese year.

steps.why: The shortest day and longest night of the year has been marked since prehistory as the point when daylight begins to increase; Newgrange and Stonehenge are aligned with it.
Rome's festival of Saturn ran for seven days to 23 December, with a public banquet, gift-giving, gambling and masters serving their slaves at table.
The pre-Christian religion of Scandinavia worshipped Odin, Thor, Freyr and Freyja with sacrifices and feasts led by chieftains and kings.
Feasting, ceremonial drinking and oath swearing were central to this Germanic winter festival, which merged with Christmas and still names it in Northern European languages.
Slavic rulers adopted Christianity between 863 and 988, but popular resistance lasted for centuries and the old rites lived on in a “double faith”.
The Slavic name for the days from Christmas to Epiphany covers rituals of which some date to pre-Christian times, among them carols sung from house to house for gifts.
On the longest night of the year families in Iran and its neighbours gather to eat, drink and read Hafez; in Zoroastrian tradition the night was inauspicious.
Punjab marks the passing of the winter solstice with bonfires, festive foods, bhangra and songs of Dulla Bhatti on the night before Makar Sankranti.
China's winter solstice festival, first celebrated under the Zhou and made official under the Han, reads the lengthening days through yin and yang.
Japan closes the year with house cleaning, repaid debts and long noodles, and at midnight most Buddhist temples strike a large bell 108 times.

title: The Story of Christmas
tagline: From the Nativity accounts and the choice of 25 December to the customs of the feast.
intro: Christmas commemorates the birth of Jesus, told in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, which state no date. The earliest document to place the birth on 25 December was written in Rome in 336; the day was the traditional date of the winter solstice in the Roman Empire. These stops begin with the faith and the Nativity accounts, then follow the customs that gathered around the feast: the manger scene attributed to Francis of Assisi in 1223, carols, the tree first recorded among German Lutherans in the 16th century, and the gift-bringer who grew from a 4th-century bishop of Myra into Santa Claus. The last stop is Dickens's novella of 1843.

steps.why: The faith began among the followers of Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish teacher crucified around 30 CE, and became the religion of the Roman Empire in the 4th century.
Matthew and Luke agree that Jesus was born in Bethlehem in the reign of Herod but state no date; only Matthew has the wise men, only Luke the shepherds.
The magi were priests of Zoroastrianism and earlier Iranian religions; in Matthew, magi from the east pay homage to the infant Jesus, rendered in English as kings or wise men.
The earliest document to place the birth on 25 December was written in Rome in 336; the day was the traditional date of the winter solstice in the Roman Empire.
The 4th-century bishop of Myra was venerated as a wonder-worker and patron of sailors and children, and from 1087 his shrine at Bari drew pilgrims.
The first seasonal manger scene, enacted rather than sculpted, is attributed to Francis of Assisi, who is said to have staged it in a cave near Greccio in 1223.
Christmas hymns may be traced to 4th-century Rome and the earliest English carols to a manuscript of 1426; carols grew in popularity after the Reformation.
The decorated evergreen was first recorded among German Lutherans in the 16th century, and in Britain Queen Charlotte introduced a tree in 1800.
The gift-bringer of Christmas Eve derives from Saint Nicholas and the Dutch Sinterklaas; an 1823 poem with a sleigh and flying reindeer laid the foundation of his modern image.
Dickens's novella of the miser Scrooge and the three spirits was published on 19 December 1843, sold out by Christmas Eve and has never been out of print.

title: Winter at War
tagline: Campaigns and sieges that ice, snow, cold and hunger decided or shaped.
intro: Winter has served some armies and destroyed others. In 1242 Alexander Nevsky defeated the Livonian Order on frozen Lake Peipus, and in 1658 a Swedish king marched across the frozen Belts to force a treaty on Denmark. These stops then follow the frosts of 1708–1709 that killed thousands in the Swedish army invading Russia, Washington's crossing of the icy Delaware and the winter camp at Valley Forge, and the retreat of 1812 that destroyed most of Napoleon's army. The last stops are the Finnish ski troops of the Winter War and the siege of Leningrad, where many residents starved in the winter of 1941–1942.

steps.why: On 5 April 1242 Alexander Nevsky's Novgorodians defeated the Livonian Order on frozen Lake Peipus, which checked the crusaders' expansion into Russian lands.
In 1658 Charles X Gustav marched across the frozen Belts and forced the Treaty of Roskilde on Denmark; in 1709 defeat at Poltava broke Swedish power.
In Europe's coldest winter of the past 500 years, storms and frosts killed thousands in the Swedish army invading Russia, contributing to its defeat at Poltava.
On the night of 25–26 December 1776 Washington led a column across the icy Delaware in rain, sleet and snow to surprise the Hessians at Trenton.
In winter quarters from December 1777 an estimated 1,700 to 2,000 soldiers died of disease, possibly made worse by malnutrition and cold, wet weather.
The empire proclaimed in 1721 after the defeat of Sweden was invaded in 1812 by Napoleon's Grande Armée, which was destroyed in the winter retreat.
The Russian army retreated and fought at Borodino, Moscow burned after its occupation, and Napoleon's retreat in winter destroyed most of his army.
Independent since 1917, Finland was attacked by the Soviet Union in 1939 and fought the Winter War, losing Karelia but keeping its independence.
From December 1939 Finnish ski troops cut two road-bound Soviet divisions into isolated pockets in the forests of north-eastern Finland and destroyed them.
The Germans decided to starve the city: many residents starved in the winter of 1941–1942, and supplies crossed Lake Ladoga in winter over the Road of Life on the ice.
